newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police believe kidnap victim's body found.
newsitem.headline: German police believe kidnap victim's body found.

text.p: Lingering hopes of finding German kidnap victim Jakub Fiszman alive appeared dashed on Saturday when police said they had found a corpse which was almost certainly that of the multi-millionaire businessman.
After an exhaustive four-day search in dense woodland outside Frankfurt, police said they had found a body lying face down and partly covered by leaves and a felled tree.

"According to the information we have so far, we believe that in all probability, verging on certainty, the body is that of Jakub Fiszman," Klaus Timm, police chief in Hesse state, told a news conference.
The search for Fiszman had gripped Germany for days and involved hundreds of police, aided by sniffer dogs and even Tornado reconnaissance jets.
Fiszman, 40, whose family fortune has been put at over 400 million marks ($250 million) but who kept out of the public eye, was abducted outside his office in Frankfurt on October 1.
The last sign that he was alive came when he made a telephone call to a friend the following day.

Timm said an initial examiniation of the body suggested it might have lain in the same place for several weeks. "I can't make any statement on the cause of death or whether he was killed where he was found," he said.
He said a final identification had not yet taken place but the clothes on the body matched a description of what Fiszman was wearing when he was kidnapped.

Two suspects, Rainer Koerppen, 48, and his son Sven, 26, have been in custody since Wednesday. Timm said police were able to narrow down the search area after Sven Koerppen gave them more information on Friday night.
Fiszman's brother Georg paid a ransom of four million marks ($2.50 million) on October 10, but his kidnappers reneged on an agreement and failed to free him on the following day.
Police have recovered most of the ransom from the garden of an apartment in Wiesbaden owned by Rainer Koerppen's parents.

Rainer Koerppen has denied all allegations, but his son confessed on Friday to being involved in the kidnapping. He told police that he and his father drove Fiszman to woodland near Frankfurt on October 4.
"Sven said he waited in the car while his father walked away with Fiszman and came back after 45 minutes," Timm said. They then drove back without speaking about the matter.

Timm said the son told police his father's mask had slipped during an initial scuffle when they kidnapped Fiszman, enabling the victim to catch a glimpse of his captor. This could have been a motive for killing Fiszman, Timm said.
Police said they were looking for at least one other kidnapper.

Fiszman, son of a Jewish immigrant from Poland who built the family's business empire in electronic goods trading and real estate, was aware of the dangers inherent in his wealth but did not employ bodyguards.
Fiszman's nephew, then aged six, was abducted in 1991 and released after three days. Media reports said the family paid one million marks ($650,000) for his freedom.
Police have said there were certain details in a letter from Fiszman' abductors that could only have been known to the 1991 kidnappers.
